Females of the Dark-spotted frog Pelophylax nigromaculatus attain a maximum snout-vent length of 10.5 cm [Li = 10.5 cm], while males reach a somewhat smaller ultimate snout-vent length of 9 cm [Li = 9 cm], reflecting a common pattern of sexual size dimorphism among ranid frogs. Field surveys and measurements from preserved museum specimens indicate that the body mass of fully grown adult females reaches an ultimate wet weight of approximately 118 grams [Wwi = approximately 118 grams], a value that is consistent with allometric predictions derived from congeneric species of similar body dimensions. This substantial adult size contrasts markedly with the modest mass observed at the earliest life stages, when newly hatched individuals emerge from their jelly-coated eggs. At the moment of eclosion, which involves the rupture of the chorion and the gelatinous capsule, the hatchlings weigh only 0.0063 grams [Wwb = 0.0063 grams], a figure that underscores the extreme ontogenetic growth trajectory that characterizes this semi-aquatic amphibian throughout its larval and post-metamorphic development.

The period of embryonic development within the aquatic egg is relatively brief, with egg hatching occurring after approximately 8 days [ab = approximately 8 days] when maintained at a constant incubation temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. Following chorion rupture, the yolk-sac larva enters an endotrophic phase during which it relies entirely on endogenous yolk reserves for sustenance, a stage that persists until the mouth opens and the onset of exogenous feeding begins. The lecithotrophic tadpole gradually transitions into an actively filter-feeding aquatic larva that grazes on algae and detritus. As the Gosner-stage larva progresses through its growth phase, it undergoes a dramatic increase in body dimensions. By the time the tadpole reaches metamorphic climax, characterized by limb bud development, tail resorption, and gill resorption, it attains a snout-vent length of 1.9 cm , and its wet weight at metamorphosis is 0.7 grams . This mass at the completion of larval metamorphosis represents a substantial gain over the hatchling weight, reflecting the period of intensive feeding and somatic growth in the aquatic environment.

Upon completion of the larval-juvenile transition, the post-metamorphic juvenile, or froglet, emerges onto land and enters a phase of rapid terrestrial growth. Field records and mark-recapture studies indicate that these immature post-metamorphic individuals attain sexual maturity, marked by the onset of gametogenesis and gonadal maturation, at a snout-vent length of 5.8 cm [Lp = 5.8 cm]. The wet weight at puberty for both sexes has been estimated at 20 grams [Wwp = 20 grams], a value that represents roughly one-sixth of the ultimate adult mass. However, the timing of this reproductive maturation differs between the sexes under standard thermal conditions. At a mean environmental temperature of 17.1 °C [T = 17.1 °C], female Pelophylax nigromaculatus reach sexual maturity at approximately 3 years following metamorphosis [tp = approximately 3 years following metamorphosis], whereas males mature more rapidly, achieving puberty at about 2 years following metamorphosis [tp = about 2 years following metamorphosis]. This sexual divergence in maturation time is a common life-history strategy among temperate anurans, likely driven by differential selective pressures on body size at first reproduction. During the peak breeding season, gravid females produce between 1,500 and 2,000 eggs per clutch, a substantial fecundity that is typical of explosive-breeding ranids. Under optimal thermal conditions at 17.1 °C [T = 17.1 °C], females typically deposit approximately 1.5 clutches per year, a rate that maximizes annual reproductive success while allowing sufficient time for somatic recovery and foraging between successive oviposition events.

The maximum lifespan of Pelophylax nigromaculatus under natural conditions has been documented at approximately 15 years [am = approximately 15 years], based on long-term field observations of marked individuals in stable pond habitats at a mean water temperature of 17.1 °C [T = 17.1 °C]. This longevity is relatively high compared to many small-bodied temperate anurans and reflects a life-history strategy oriented toward iteroparity. The reproductive output associated with this extended adult phase can be estimated from the maximum daily egg production rate, which field studies suggest corresponds to an annual output on the order of several thousand eggs per female — a level of fecundity that is typical of explosive-breeding ranids and is energetically supported by the substantial body reserves accumulated during the foraging period.

Comparative analyses with other members of the genus Pelophylax reveal that the Dark-spotted frog exhibits a relatively protracted lifespan and delayed maturity relative to its body size, a pattern consistent with a slow-paced life history. The species also shows notable plasticity in its developmental rates, as tadpoles reared at cooler temperatures exhibit slower growth and later metamorphosis, an adaptation that allows populations to persist across a wide latitudinal gradient in East Asia. Further ecological studies are needed to clarify the relationship between thermal regime and reproductive scheduling in this widespread anuran.
